481.quote_or_event: “He could appoint a worm as king, and reduce an army to ashes.”
481.explanation: In Majh Ki Vaar Guru Nanak says that God can raise the weakest creature to a throne and bring the mightiest army to nothing.
481.tie_back: The Kural shows the weaker crow beating the stronger owl when the hour favours it; Guru Nanak also sees the weak overturning the strong, though by God's will rather than timing.
481.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 144, Raag Maajh, Majh Ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
481._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the reversal of strength is shared, but Gurbani credits it to divine command, not to choosing the right time.

482.quote_or_event: “This human body has been given to you. This is your chance to meet the Lord of the Universe.”
482.explanation: In a hymn recited daily in Rehras, Guru Arjan tells the soul that the human birth is its ripe moment, the opportunity not to be let slip.
482.tie_back: The Kural says acting in step with the season is the rope that holds Fortune fast; Guru Arjan calls human life the one season in which the highest prize can be won.
482.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12, Raag Aasaa (So Purakh / Rehras), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
482._accuracy_note: Reasonable: both stress seizing the right season, but Gurbani's opportunity is union with God, not worldly fortune.

483.quote_or_event: “My strength has been restored, and my bonds have been broken; now, I can do everything.”
483.explanation: This salok answers the preceding cry of helplessness: with strength restored through God, every means (upai) becomes possible. Some traditions attribute it to Guru Gobind Singh, though the Guru Granth Sahib places it among Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks.
483.tie_back: The Kural asks whether anything is impossible for one with the right means at the right time; the salok declares that with strength and means restored, everything can be done.
483.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1429, Salok Mahalla 9 (salok 54) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
483._accuracy_note: Partial: the sense that nothing is impossible with means in hand fits, but the salok credits God's grace and says nothing about timing; its authorship is traditionally discussed.

484.quote_or_event: Ranjit Singh rose to pre-eminence among the clans of the Sikh confederacy, captured Lahore in 1799 and went on to extend his rule across the Punjab, founding the Sikh kingdom over which he ruled as maharaja.
484.explanation: Starting as one chief among many, Ranjit Singh built a kingdom out of a divided Punjab by moving at the right moment and from the right base.
484.tie_back: The Kural says even the whole world can be won by one who picks the right time and place; Ranjit Singh's rise from Lahore to rule of the Punjab is a Sikh historical case of such a gain.
484.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Ranjit Singh" by Khushwant Singh (paraphrase)
484._accuracy_note: Next-best only: political history, not Sikh teaching; the source summary confirms the capture of Lahore (1799) but not the specific timing judgements the Kural stresses.

485.quote_or_event: “Within yourself, make patience the bow, and make patience the bowstring. Make patience the arrow, the Creator will not let you miss the target.”
485.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose saloks are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, makes patience (sabar) the whole weapon: bow, string and arrow, which God will not let miss.
485.tie_back: The Kural shows those who aim at the world waiting calmly and unshaken for their time; Farid teaches that patience itself is the weapon that finds its mark.
485.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 115) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
485._accuracy_note: A strong fit on patient, unshaken waiting that does not miss; Farid's target is spiritual, not dominion over the world.

486.quote_or_event: “The sinner, like the deer hunter, bows down twice as much.”
486.explanation: In Asa Ki Vaar Guru Nanak notes that a hunter stalking deer bends low only to strike, so outward bowing is no proof of humility.
486.tie_back: The Kural compares the energetic man's holding back to a ram stepping back before it charges; Guru Nanak sees the same pattern in the hunter's crouch before the kill.
486.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Aasaa, Asa Ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
486._accuracy_note: The image of drawing in before striking matches, but Guru Nanak uses it to expose false humility, while the Kural commends the tactic.

487.quote_or_event: “O anger, you are the root of conflict; compassion never rises up in you.”
487.explanation: In the Salok Sehskritee, Guru Arjan addresses anger (krodh), one of the five thieves, as the root of strife and the enemy of compassion.
487.tie_back: The Kural has the wise keep their anger hidden until the right time; Sikh teaching goes further and treats anger itself as a vice to be overcome, not stored up.
487.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1358, Salok Sehskritee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
487._accuracy_note: Mainly a contrast: the Kural counsels hiding anger for strategic use, whereas Gurbani condemns anger outright as one of the five thieves.

488.quote_or_event: “Fareed, do not turn around and strike those who strike you with their fists. Kiss their feet, and return to your own home.”
488.explanation: Sheikh Farid tells the seeker not to return blows but to answer aggressors with deference and go home in peace.
488.tie_back: The Kural says to bear with foes and even honour them until their time of downfall comes; Farid also counsels bearing foes and honouring them.
488.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 7) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
488._accuracy_note: The outward conduct matches, but the motive is opposite: Farid gives up revenge, while the Kural defers it until the enemy can be struck down.

489.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, that which you have to do tomorrow - do it today instead; and that which you have to do now - do it immediately! Later on, you will not be able to do anything, when death hangs over your head.”
489.explanation: Bhagat Kabir urges acting at once while the chance remains, because the moment, once lost, does not return.
489.tie_back: The Kural says to seize a rare opportunity the moment it comes and do the hard deed; Kabir insists on acting now, before the opening closes.
489.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1371, Salok Bhagat Kabir (salok 138) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
489._accuracy_note: A strong fit on acting immediately when the chance is present; Kabir's urgency comes from death and is aimed at devotion, not at a rare worldly opening.

490.quote_or_event: “Fareed, the crane perches on the river bank, playing joyfully. While it is playing, a hawk suddenly pounces on it.”
490.explanation: Sheikh Farid's crane sits heedless on the riverbank until a hawk falls on it without warning, an image of death striking the careless.
490.tie_back: The Kural tells one to wait like a heron and strike like its beak when the moment comes; Farid uses the same waterside bird, but as the prey of a sudden strike rather than the striker.
490.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1383, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
490._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the heron or crane and the sudden strike are shared, but Farid reverses the roles and warns of death, not of timing one's attack.
